svg.title: DDIA 2 · DEFINING NONFUNCTIONAL REQUIREMENTS: sketchnote
svg.text: How fast, how dependable, how it grows, how easy to run and change: each turned into a number.
celebrities: skip fan-out, merge their posts at read
push = ~1M cache writes/s. Celebrities merged at read time.
Under load the queue grows first: a server at 90% busy makes requests wait far longer than they take to process.
Response = network + queueing + service time. Queues grow
first under load, so measure on the client.
A blip, then timeouts, then retries keep it overloaded. Backoff
+ jitter, retry budgets, circuit breakers, load shedding.
The user waits for the slowest backend. With 100 backends at
1% slow each, 63% of user requests hit at least one slow call.
A failure is when the whole system stops serving users. You
design so faults don't become failures.
~1 in 1,000 machines: a CPU core that
config changes: the #1 cause of outages
the 32,768-hour SSD bug), so replicas do not
help. Blameless postmortems fix the process.
simple; one box is the limit
scales furthest; all of Part II
Scale up first. Shared-nothing scales furthest but brings all of
Part II. Rethink at every 10× of load.
Name the load parameter (reads/sec, fan-out, data size),
calculate it, then say which component breaks first.
p99 < 200ms for reads, not averages. Mention tail amplification
Separate fault from failure: "A node dying is a fault. Replicas
plus health checks mean it never becomes a failure."
"Before choosing components, let me pin down the load
parameters: DAU, read:write ratio, and peak QPS, because
they decide whether we need any distribution at all."
Study notes on Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition (Kleppmann & Riccomini). Read the book.
